episodes.series_title: The Crows That Never Forgot a Face
episodes.episode_title: The Man in the Caveman Mask
episodes.youtube_title: The Crows That Never Forgot a Face (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: Crows can hold a grudge against a human face for years. One scientist proved it with a caveman mask. Biologist John Marzluff studied the crows on a Seattle university campus. His team trapped crows to band them, all while wearing that mask. They caught just seven crows, banded their legs, and let them go. Later, people wore that same mask on calm walks across campus. Crows screamed at the masked walker and gathered to mob him. But some of the scolding crows had never been trapped at all. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: But some of the scolding crows had never been trapped at all.
episodes.description: A scientist wore a caveman mask to catch a few crows, and the whole campus seemed to remember. Has a bird ever held a grudge against you?

episodes.series_title: The Crows That Never Forgot a Face
episodes.episode_title: A Grudge That Spread
episodes.youtube_title: The Crows That Never Forgot a Face (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Crows that were never caught learned to hate the mask anyway. In Part 1, scientists trapped seven crows while wearing a caveman mask. Walkers also wore a neutral mask, and crows mostly ignored it. The caveman face alone set them off. For seven years, more and more crows joined in. Scientists found evidence that crows learned by watching others scold. Across twelve years, roughly four in ten crows they passed scolded the caveman. Then scientists looked inside crow brains to see what that face did. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: Then scientists looked inside crow brains to see what that face did.
episodes.description: Crows that were never caught still scolded the caveman mask, and the grudge kept spreading for years. Do you think crows gossip?

episodes.series_title: The Crows That Never Forgot a Face
episodes.episode_title: Inside a Crow's Grudge
episodes.youtube_title: The Crows That Never Forgot a Face (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Crow brains react to a dangerous face much like ours do. In Part 2, crows that were never caught learned to scold the mask. In a later study, researchers scanned the brains of captive wild crows. Crows saw a mask linked to capture, or one linked to feeding. The threatening face lit up regions tied to emotion, much like our amygdala. Back on campus, the caveman kept getting scolded for years. Nearly two decades after the trapping, crows finally ignored him. Wrong a crow, and the whole flock may remember. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: Brain scans showed a scary face lighting up emotion areas in crow brains, and the campus grudge lasted nearly two decades. Would you want a crow as a friend or an enemy?

episodes.youtube_title: The Ranger Lightning Hit Seven Times (Part 2/3)

The truck strike knocked him out and set his hair on fire. The next summer, lightning hit a transformer in his yard and jumped to his shoulder. Then a bolt set his hair on fire again, at a ranger station. Another knocked his shoe off while he was on patrol. Even his wife was struck once, while hanging laundry in the yard. And his seventh strike came on a fishing trip. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: And his seventh strike came on a fishing trip.
episodes.description: His truck, his yard, a ranger station, even his wife hanging laundry. Lightning kept finding Roy Sullivan. Would you ever go outside in a storm again?

Reports say a bear came for his fish, and he hit it with a branch. The weather service puts the lifetime odds of being struck at about one in 15,000. But most people struck are outdoors, working or having fun, like fishing. And he spent decades working outdoors in the mountains. Lightning never strikes twice? Tell that to Roy Sullivan. episodes.description: Seven strikes, a bear on a fishing trip, and odds of about one in 15,000 for the rest of us. What is the closest call you have had with a storm?

And she remembered one rule her father had taught her. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.

episodes.youtube_title: The Teen Who Fell From the Sky and Lived (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Her father's survival rule was to follow the water downstream. In Part 1, a 17-year-old fell from a plane into the Amazon. She had a broken collarbone and a deep cut on her arm. She found a small stream and followed it through the rainforest. Her parents were biologists, so she knew the jungle's sounds. Her only food was a bag of candy from the crash. Her wounded arm became badly infected. Then, after more than a week, she found a boat, and a hut. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.

By her own account, she poured it on her infected arm. Then the men who used the hut came back. They took her by canoe to get help. Juliane Koepcke became a biologist, and now runs her parents' research station in the Amazon. The jungle that nearly killed her became her life's work. Subscribe for a new true story every day.

episodes.script: The movie Balto was loosely based on a real race against death. And the dog who ran the hardest miles isn't the one who got famous. In the winter of 1925, diphtheria hit Nome, Alaska, putting its children in danger. Nome's medicine had expired. The sea was frozen, so no ship could reach the town until spring. A train brought fresh medicine to a town still 674 miles away. The rest of the way, it would travel by dog sled. And the most dangerous stretch would go to a 12-year-old dog. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.

Twenty mushers and their dogs passed it from team to team, in cold as low as minus 60 degrees Fahrenheit. The longest stretch went to musher Leonhard Seppala and his lead dog, Togo. To save time, Togo led the team across the sea ice. And that ice was breaking up. Togo got them across. But the dog who became world famous was one Seppala had left behind. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.

But the final leg was led by Balto, and he became a celebrity. That December, a statue of him was unveiled in New York's Central Park, with Balto there. According to Seppala, Balto was one of his own freight dogs, one he had left behind. He was heartbroken that the credit went to Balto instead. Balto got the statue, but Togo ran the hardest miles. episodes.script: Experts once said sharks posed almost no danger off New Jersey. One summer shattered that belief, and it's still widely linked to Jaws. It was July 1916. A heat wave and a polio outbreak had crowds rushing to the Jersey Shore. At Beach Haven, a young man was attacked in the surf and died. Five days later, at Spring Lake, a hotel worker was killed too. Beach towns were terrified. Yet some experts still doubted a shark was even to blame. And the next victims weren't swimming in the ocean at all. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.

episodes.youtube_title: The Shark Attacks Everyone Links to Jaws (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: The next attacks came in a small creek, miles from the sea. In Part 1, two swimmers died at Jersey Shore beaches, and experts doubted sharks. On July 12, boys were swimming in Matawan Creek when a shark attacked Lester Stillwell, age 11. A local man, Stanley Fisher, dove in to find him. He was bitten and later died. Within the hour, a shark attacked another boy nearby. Joseph Dunn survived. Towns fenced off swimming spots and dynamited the creek. Two days later, a shark was caught a few miles away, with a grim surprise inside. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: Two days later, a shark was caught a few miles away, with a grim surprise inside.

episodes.youtube_title: The Shark Attacks Everyone Links to Jaws (Part 3/3)

The caught shark was a young great white, and experts back then declared it the man-eater. But shark experts today still question how reliable those old reports were. Some suspect a bull shark instead, because bull sharks can swim into fresher water. The debate has never been settled. And Jaws? These attacks are widely credited with inspiring it. Yet author Peter Benchley denied that link. The most unbelievable part is the part that really happened. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: The shark caught after the 1916 attacks may not have been the killer, and the Jaws author denied any link. Great white or bull shark, what do you think?

episodes.youtube_title: The Ice Took Their Ship but Not One Man (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: The most famous job ad in exploration history may never have existed. It supposedly promised bitter cold, and that safe return was doubtful. Historians have hunted for the original for years, and never found it. But the voyage it's linked to was very real. In 1914, Ernest Shackleton sailed for Antarctica on a ship called Endurance. Then sea ice closed in around it, trapping the ship for months. The ice slowly crushed its wooden hull. And when it sank, 28 men were stranded on the frozen sea. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: And when it sank, 28 men were stranded on the frozen sea.

episodes.youtube_title: The Ice Took Their Ship but Not One Man (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Their ship was gone, so they lived on floating ice for months. In Part 1, sea ice crushed Shackleton's ship, Endurance. The men camped in tents on the drifting ice. When the ice broke apart, they took three small boats to a rocky, empty island. Then Shackleton and five men sailed a tiny lifeboat 800 miles through stormy seas to find help. After more than two weeks, they reached the island of South Georgia. But the only help was on the other side of its icy mountains. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: But the only help was on the other side of its icy mountains.

episodes.youtube_title: The Ice Took Their Ship but Not One Man (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Three exhausted men crossed icy mountains to save everyone they'd left behind. In Part 2, Shackleton sailed a tiny lifeboat to South Georgia. He and two men climbed over its glaciers and walked into a whaling station. Then Shackleton went back for the men on the island. It took months, but every single one of the 28 men survived. And in 2022, searchers found Endurance about 3,000 meters down. The icy water had kept it remarkably well preserved, with its name still visible. They lost their ship, but not one man. episodes.description: Every one of the 28 men made it home, and in 2022 their lost ship was found deep under the Weddell Sea. What would you want to see on that wreck?

episodes.episode_title: Millions of Butterflies Gone Missing

episodes.script: Millions of butterflies disappeared every fall, and scientists couldn't find them. Monarchs flew south from Canada and the United States, then seemed to vanish. A Canadian zoologist, Fred Urquhart, spent decades trying to follow them. He stuck tiny tags on their wings, printed with his office address. Volunteers across North America joined in, tagging butterflies. The trail led to Texas, then pointed into Mexico. His wife, Norah, placed an ad in a Mexican newspaper asking for help. One reply would lead to a mountain covered in orange wings. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.

episodes.episode_title: The Mountain Covered in Monarchs
episodes.youtube_title: The Hidden Forest Where Monarchs Go (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: The butterflies were hiding on a mountain in central Mexico. In Part 1, a scientist's newspaper ad asked for help finding the monarchs. Ken Brugger and Catalina Aguado searched the mountains for years. In January 1975, they reached a high forest of fir trees. Millions of monarchs covered the branches, trunks and even the ground. Amazingly, Brugger was colorblind and couldn't see their famous orange. Later, Fred Urquhart found one there that was tagged in Minnesota. But no butterfly that makes this trip has ever made it before. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: But no butterfly that makes this trip has ever made it before.

episodes.youtube_title: The Hidden Forest Where Monarchs Go (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Each monarch flies to a forest it has never seen. In Part 2, volunteers found millions of monarchs in Mexico's mountain forests. Summer monarchs live only a few weeks. But the fall super generation can live up to eight months. They steer with a sun compass, timed by clocks in their antennae. They arrive around early November, as Mexico celebrates the Day of the Dead. In many communities, they're seen as the souls of loved ones returning. They've never been there, yet they arrive right on time. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: A super generation of monarchs lives months longer than its parents and reaches Mexico just in time for the Day of the Dead. Have you ever seen a monarch?

episodes.script: Nineteen men fell from the Golden Gate Bridge and lived. In the 1930s, working on high steel was deadly. Men worked hundreds of feet up, over cold, rough water. The grim rule of thumb was one worker killed for every million dollars spent. This bridge would cost about 35 million. But its chief engineer, Joseph Strauss, pushed for strict safety rules. His bridge was among the first job sites in America to require hard hats. And under the bridge, he hung something that would save lives. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.

The net cost about 130,000 dollars, in the middle of the Great Depression. It hung under the workers, high above the cold water of the bay. During construction, 19 men fell into that net and survived. They joked that they had only fallen halfway to hell. So they called themselves the Halfway to Hell Club. Ten men died, and only two survived. Three months later, the bridge opened to huge crowds. A plaque still honors the men who died. The net saved 19 lives, but it couldn't save them all. episodes.script: Villagers dug up a teenage girl's grave to stop a vampire. And this wasn't the Middle Ages. It was 1892, in Rhode Island. A disease called consumption had already killed Mercy Brown's mother and older sister. That winter, it killed Mercy too, at just 19. Now her brother Edwin was seriously ill. Consumption seemed to drain the life and blood out of its victims. So neighbors came up with a chilling theory: one of the dead Brown women was feeding on Edwin. episodes.youtube_title: The Girl They Dug Up to Stop a Vampire (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Mercy's heart still held blood, months after she died. In Part 1, neighbors decided a dead relative was feeding on Mercy's brother. So villagers, with a doctor and a reporter, opened the graves. Mercy had died in midwinter, and her body was fairly well preserved. To the villagers, that looked like proof. So they burned her heart and liver on a nearby rock. They mixed the ashes with water and gave them to Edwin as a cure. Years later, a clipping about New England's vampires turned up in the papers of Dracula's author. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.

episodes.youtube_title: The Girl They Dug Up to Stop a Vampire (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Bram Stoker's papers held a clipping about New England's vampires. In Part 2, villagers burned Mercy Brown's heart and fed the ashes to her sick brother. That clipping ran the year before Stoker published Dracula. Some scholars see Mercy in Dracula's Lucy, a young woman turned vampire and dug up. Others say there wasn't enough time. Either way, the ritual failed, and her brother died less than two months later. The real killer was tuberculosis, the disease they called consumption. The monster was never in the grave. It was in their lungs. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: A clipping about New England's vampires ended up in Bram Stoker's papers, and some scholars see Mercy Brown in Dracula. Do you think she inspired Lucy?

episodes.series_title: The Volcano Behind Frankenstein
episodes.episode_title: The Volcano That Stole Summer
episodes.youtube_title: The Volcano Behind Frankenstein (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: A volcano helped create the monster behind del Toro's Frankenstein. In 1815, Mount Tambora exploded in what's now Indonesia. It was the largest eruption in recorded history. Its ash rose high, and the next year became the Year Without a Summer. Snow fell in parts of New York and Maine in June. Frost killed crops, and food riots broke out in Europe. In Switzerland, cold, stormy weather trapped a group of young writers indoors by Lake Geneva. And one of them, just 18 years old, was about to dream up a monster. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: And one of them, just 18 years old, was about to dream up a monster.
episodes.description: A volcano in Indonesia wiped out summer on the other side of the world and trapped a group of young writers indoors. What would you write on a stormy night?

episodes.series_title: The Volcano Behind Frankenstein
episodes.episode_title: The Ghost Story Dare That Made Frankenstein
episodes.youtube_title: The Volcano Behind Frankenstein (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Frankenstein began as an 18-year-old's answer to a ghost story challenge. In Part 1, a volcano's freezing summer trapped young writers indoors by Lake Geneva. At Lord Byron's villa, the poet proposed they each write a ghost story. Mary Godwin, the future Mary Shelley, struggled at first. Then one night, she had what she later called a waking dream. She pictured a pale student kneeling beside a creature he had built. That vision became the seed of Frankenstein. But Byron's own doctor would turn the same challenge into a very different monster. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: But Byron's own doctor would turn the same challenge into a very different monster.
episodes.description: Lord Byron challenged his friends to write ghost stories, and an 18-year-old dreamed up Frankenstein. What is the scariest story you ever heard?

episodes.series_title: The Volcano Behind Frankenstein
episodes.episode_title: The Other Monster Born That Summer
episodes.youtube_title: The Volcano Behind Frankenstein (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: That same ghost story challenge also helped create the modern vampire. In Part 2, Byron's challenge sparked the idea for Frankenstein. Byron started a vampire tale, but he never finished it. His doctor, John Polidori, built on that fragment and wrote The Vampyre. Its vampire was a charming aristocrat, a model that helped shape Dracula. But it was wrongly credited to Byron. And Frankenstein came out with no author's name at all. Many readers assumed Mary's husband wrote it. Two monsters were born that summer, and neither got its author's name. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: The stormy summer that sparked Frankenstein also gave the world a charming vampire, and neither book carried its real author's name. Which monster scares you more?

episodes.series_title: The Martian Panic That Barely Happened
episodes.episode_title: Martians on the Radio
episodes.youtube_title: The Martian Panic That Barely Happened (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: Before Spielberg's War of the Worlds, a radio version supposedly panicked America. The evidence tells a different story. The night before Halloween in 1938, Orson Welles aired his version on CBS radio. Dance music kept getting cut off by fake news bulletins. Reporters described a strange object landing in New Jersey. Anyone who tuned in late could wait almost 40 minutes to hear it was fiction. By morning, newspapers across the country were reporting mass panic. But a ratings survey that night found only a tiny share of homes were even listening. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.
episodes.cliffhanger: But a ratings survey that night found only a tiny share of homes were even listening.
episodes.description: The night before Halloween, a radio drama told America that Martians had landed in New Jersey. Would you have fallen for it?

episodes.series_title: The Martian Panic That Barely Happened
episodes.episode_title: The Ratings That Sank the Panic Story
episodes.youtube_title: The Martian Panic That Barely Happened (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Almost no one surveyed that night was listening to the Martian invasion. In Part 1, newspapers claimed a Martian radio drama had panicked America. A ratings service surveyed 5,000 homes, and just 2 percent were listening to Welles. Yet within three weeks, newspapers ran at least 12,500 articles about the broadcast. Later, a Princeton study estimated over a million people were frightened. But it relied on audience numbers far higher than other surveys found. And being scared isn't the same as panicking. Meanwhile, newspapers were losing money to the very thing they blamed. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: Meanwhile, newspapers were losing money to the very thing they blamed.
episodes.description: Newspapers ran thousands of stories about a nationwide panic, but a survey from that night found almost nobody listening. Do you trust old headlines?

episodes.series_title: The Martian Panic That Barely Happened
episodes.episode_title: Why Newspapers Blew It Up
episodes.youtube_title: The Martian Panic That Barely Happened (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: The great Martian panic story may have been about advertising money. In Part 2, a survey found only 2 percent of homes were listening to the broadcast. During the Great Depression, radio had been pulling advertising money away from newspapers. Two media scholars argue newspapers seized the chance to paint radio as irresponsible and unreliable. And many of the panic stories fell apart. No deaths or suicides linked to the show were ever verified. Some listeners truly were scared. The Martians landed on radio. The panic mostly landed in newspapers. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: Radio was taking newspapers' advertising money, and some scholars say that is why the War of the Worlds panic became a legend. Did you believe the panic story?

episodes.youtube_title: The Escape Houdini Never Made (Part 1/3)
episodes.script: The world's most famous escape artist died on Halloween. Days earlier, a college student had punched him in the stomach. The student had visited his dressing room in Montreal, asking if punches really didn't hurt Houdini. Then, without warning, he struck several times while Houdini was lying on a couch. That evening, the pain began and got worse. Houdini still traveled to Detroit and performed with a fever of 104 degrees. Doctors found a burst appendix, and on Halloween, the infection killed him. But the punches may not be what really killed him. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.

episodes.series_title: The Escape Houdini Never Made
episodes.episode_title: Houdini Versus the Fake Mediums
episodes.youtube_title: The Escape Houdini Never Made (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Houdini's insurance company paid out as if the punches killed him. In Part 1, Houdini died on Halloween, days after a student punched him. Doctors back then blamed the blows. But modern scholars mostly think he already had appendicitis, and the punches just made him ignore it. Houdini had also spent years exposing fake mediums who claimed to talk to the dead. He said a famous Boston medium, Margery, secretly rang a bell with her foot. But Houdini and his wife had agreed on a secret code, meant for after his death. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: But Houdini and his wife had agreed on a secret code, meant for after his death.
episodes.description: Doctors blamed a student's punches, but Houdini's death is more complicated, and so was his war on fake mediums. Do you believe anyone can talk to the dead?

episodes.series_title: The Escape Houdini Never Made
episodes.episode_title: The Final Halloween Seance
episodes.youtube_title: The Escape Houdini Never Made (Part 3/3)
episodes.script: Houdini's secret code for the afterlife was just two words. In Part 2, Houdini exposed fake mediums who claimed to speak with the dead. The code was Rosabelle, believe. Rosabelle was a song from their youth. Every year, his wife Bess held a seance, hoping to hear it. On the tenth Halloween after his death, a last seance was held on a Hollywood rooftop. Nothing came through. Bess put out the candle she had kept burning since he died. The man who exposed fake mediums got the last word: silence. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
episodes.description: Houdini and his wife shared a secret two-word code for after his death, and for ten years she waited to hear it. Would you have kept the candle burning?
